pageData.title: Ancient Britain
pageData.titleline: Ancient Britain - The History Web
pageData.para1: Ancient Britain. Ancient Britain's story is written not in books but in the ground - no pre-Roman Briton left a written word, so everything we know comes from archaeology and, increasingly, ancient DNA. Hunter-gatherers like 'Cheddar Man' (c. 8300 BC) held the island for millennia; then, around 4000 BC, farming arrived with migrants whose ancestors had come from Anatolia, and the Neolithic farmers who replaced them raised Britain's first great monuments: long barrows, stone circles, and Stonehenge itself (c. 3000-2500 BC).
pageData.para2: The Bronze Age brought another wave: the Bell Beaker people, arriving around 2500-2400 BC, replaced over 90% of the earlier population - one of the most complete population turnovers known from ancient DNA - and brought metalworking and steppe ancestry to the island. Through it all, Britain was never cut off: Cornish tin, hunting dogs, and animal skins flowed out to Europe in trade, and ideas flowed back.
pageData.para3: The Iron Age (from c. 750 BC) made Britain a land of farmers and hillforts. Iron ploughs opened new land, wheat farming flourished, and some 3,300 hillforts crowned the hilltops. Most Britons now spoke Brythonic, the ancestor of Welsh - whether we call them 'Celts' is debated, but their gold work, chariots, and tribal kingdoms were unmistakably part of the La Tene world. In the last centuries BC, Belgic tribes from Gaul crossed the Channel and settled the south.
pageData.para4: Recorded history begins with Julius Caesar's expeditions of 55-54 BC; the full Roman conquest came in AD 43. But the ancient Britons did not disappear - their language survives today in Welsh, Cornish, and Breton, and their greatest monuments, Stonehenge above all, still stand where their builders raised them five thousand years ago.

pageData.title: Archaic & Classical Greece
pageData.titleline: Archaic & Classical Greece - The History Web
pageData.para1: Archaic and Classical Greece. Between the fall of Mycenae and the conquests of Alexander, Greece passed through its two formative ages. In the Archaic period (c. 800-480 BC), the Greeks emerged from their Dark Age to build the world of the polis - the self-governing city-state. They adopted and perfected the alphabet, founded colonies across the Mediterranean and Black Sea until Greek cities ringed both, fought as citizen hoplites, founded the Olympic Games (776 BC), and, in Athens, took the first steps toward democracy under Solon and Cleisthenes, while Sparta hardened into a military society ruling the helots of Messenia.
pageData.para2: The Classical period (c. 480-323 BC) began in glory: the tiny Greek cities twice hurled back the Persian Empire - at Marathon in 490 BC, and against the great invasion of 481-479 BC that took Thermopylae but broke against the Greek alliance. The fifty years that followed were Athens' golden age: under Pericles, radical democracy governed an empire of tribute-paying allies, the Parthenon rose on the Acropolis, and tragedy, comedy, history, and philosophy - Aeschylus, Sophocles, Herodotus, Thucydides, Socrates - created much of what the West still calls civilization.
pageData.para3: The Greeks then destroyed their own supremacy. The Peloponnesian War (431-404 BC) between Athens and Sparta bled the Greek world white; Spartan and Theban hegemonies followed, each shorter and weaker than the last. Yet even as the city-states tore each other apart, Greek thought reached its peak in the schools of Plato and Aristotle.
pageData.para4: The end came from the north: Philip II of Macedon subdued the divided cities, and his son Alexander conquered Persia itself, carrying Greek culture to India. When Alexander died in 323 BC, the Classical age closed - but Hellenistic Greek became the common culture of the entire eastern Mediterranean, and through Rome, of the world.

pageData.title: Celtiberian Iberia
pageData.titleline: Celtiberian Iberia - The History Web
pageData.para1: Celtiberian Iberia. The Celtiberians were the Celtic peoples of ancient Spain - tribes of the central Iberian plateau who blended Celtic and native Iberian stock into a culture of their own. Classical writers like Strabo called them Celts outright; their language, written in an adapted Iberian script, is now classified as a Celtic language, and hundreds of their inscriptions survive. From perhaps the 6th century BC they lived in walled hilltop towns (castros and oppida) across the upper valleys of the Tagus, Douro, and Ebro, ruled by a hereditary warrior aristocracy.
pageData.para2: They were fighters above all. Celtiberian cavalry and swordsmen were famous - the Romans adopted the Celtiberian two-edged sword and the Spanish throwing spear (the lancea) - and Celtiberian warriors served as mercenaries across the Mediterranean. The dominant tribe, the Arevaci, led from the stronghold of Okilis, became the rallying point of resistance to Rome.
pageData.para3: That resistance was ferocious and long. Rome conquered part of Celtiberia in 195 BC, but the tribes rose again and again - in 195-193, 181-179, 153-151, and 143-133 BC - in wars that cost Rome generations of soldiers. In 105 BC Celtiberian warriors even drove the Germanic Cimbri out of Spain. Not until 72 BC, after the Sertorian War, was the whole region finally pacified as part of the Roman province of Hispania Citerior.
pageData.para4: Under Rome, Celtiberia Romanized - its towns became Roman cities, its language faded into Latin - but the fierce independence of the mountain tribes never quite died. The Celtiberians left Spain two enduring inheritances: a tradition of guerrilla resistance to empires, and place names and inscriptions that still mark the high meseta where they held out for over a century.

pageData.title: Celtic Gaul
pageData.titleline: Celtic Gaul - The History Web
pageData.para1: Celtic Gaul. Celtic Gaul was the land of the Gauls - the Celtic peoples who, in the centuries before Rome, dominated Western Europe from the Atlantic to the Rhine. Emerging with the La Tene culture around the 5th century BC, they spread over modern France, Belgium, Switzerland, and beyond, controlling the great river trade routes of the Rhone, Seine, Rhine, and Danube. Gaul was never a single state: it was a patchwork of dozens of tribes, each with its own chiefs, fortified towns (oppida like Bibracte), and coinage - sharing a language, a religion overseen by druids, and a warrior culture that made their name feared across the ancient world.
pageData.para2: At their peak in the 4th and 3rd centuries BC, the Gauls exploded outward. They settled northern Italy and, under the war leader Brennus, crushed a Roman army and sacked Rome itself in 390 BC - a humiliation Rome never forgot. Others crossed into the Balkans, threatened Delphi in 278 BC, and finally settled in central Anatolia, where they became the Galatians of the New Testament.
pageData.para3: The tide turned at Telamon in 225 BC, and a century later came the reckoning: Julius Caesar's Gallic Wars (58-50 BC). Tribe by tribe, Caesar subdued Gaul in eight brutal campaigns; the great coalition raised by the Arvernian chief Vercingetorix nearly stopped him, but broke at the siege of Alesia in 52 BC. Gaul became a Roman province - the conquest that made Caesar's career and, by Roman accounts, cost a million Gallic lives.
pageData.para4: Yet Gaul did not vanish: it fused. Out of Roman rule grew the Gallo-Roman world - cities, roads, Latin, and law laid over Celtic tradition - and eventually the very identity of France. The Gauls' language died out centuries ago, but their name lives on in 'Gaul' itself, and their fierce independence still defines how France remembers its origins.
pageData.source3label: Livius: Gaius Julius Caesar: Conquest of Gaul - Livius
pageData.source4label: National Geographic: Who were the Celts?

pageData.title: Mycenaean Greece
pageData.titleline: Mycenaean Greece - The History Web
pageData.para1: Mycenaean Greece. Mycenaean Greece (c. 1750-1050 BC) was the first great civilization of the Greek mainland - the Greece of Agamemnon, Achilles, and the Trojan War, or at least of the real Bronze Age kings behind the legends. From fortified palace-citadels at Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos, and Thebes, a warrior elite of kings (the wanax) ruled palace-centered states with rigid hierarchies, massive 'Cyclopean' walls, and tombs filled with gold.
pageData.para2: The Mycenaeans learned much from Minoan Crete and soon surpassed it: they took over Crete in the Late Bronze Age and came to dominate Aegean trade, their settlements spreading to Cyprus and the coast of Asia Minor, their pottery reaching from Italy to the Levant. They were engineers - builders of roads, bridges, drainage works, and the Lion Gate of Mycenae - and they were literate: their Linear B tablets, deciphered in 1952, are the oldest written Greek, and already name several gods later found in the Olympic pantheon - the first written evidence of Greek religion.
pageData.para3: Then, around 1200-1050 BC, the world of the palaces collapsed. Within a generation the great citadels burned, Linear B vanished, and Greece entered a four-century Dark Age. Why, no one knows: invading 'Sea Peoples,' Dorian migrants, internal revolt, drought, and systems collapse have all been blamed - probably in combination.
pageData.para4: The Mycenaeans were forgotten - but not quite. Their age lived on in memory, sung by Homer as the age of heroes: the Trojan War, if it happened, was a Mycenaean war. When Schliemann dug at Mycenae and Troy in the 1870s and found the gold, he proved that behind the legends stood a real and splendid civilization - the first chapter of Greek history.
pageData.source4label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Mycenaean Civilization

pageData.title: Roman Gaul, Britain, & Hispania
pageData.titleline: Roman Gaul, Britain, & Hispania - The History Web
pageData.para1: Roman Gaul, Britain, and Hispania. Rome's western provinces - Gaul, Britain, and Hispania - were where the Roman Empire met the Celtic world, and where Romanization did its deepest work. Hispania came first: conquered piecemeal from 218 BC, during the Second Punic War against Carthage, it took Rome two centuries of hard fighting to subdue. Gaul followed: Rome had held the Mediterranean south since 121 BC, but Caesar's conquest (58-50 BC) brought the whole country under Roman rule, reorganized under Augustus into the provinces of Aquitania, Belgica, and Lugdunensis. Britain came last: Claudius's legions landed in AD 43 and spent four decades pushing Roman rule to the edge of Scotland.
pageData.para2: For four centuries these were among the empire's most prosperous provinces. Gaul became so Roman that it gave Rome emperors - Claudius was born at Lugdunum (Lyon) - and writers like Tacitus; Hispania gave Rome Trajan, Hadrian, and Theodosius, plus the gold, silver, grain, and olive oil that fed the western empire. Roman Britain was poorer and more militarized, but it too got cities, baths, villas, and roads - and Hadrian's Wall, the empire's most famous frontier.
pageData.para3: The Roman peace changed everything: Celtic hillforts gave way to Roman towns, Latin displaced the old languages in Gaul and Spain, and local elites became Roman senators. When the western empire crumbled in the 5th century - Britain abandoned around 410, Gaul and Hispania overrun by Franks, Goths, and others - the Roman imprint remained.
pageData.para4: That imprint is still the map of Western Europe: Spanish, Portuguese, and French are Latin's daughters, London and Lyon and Cordoba are Roman foundations, and the legal and cultural DNA of the West was spliced in these provinces. The Gauls, Britons, and Iberians did not vanish - they became Roman, and then became the peoples of modern Europe.
pageData.source4label: BBC: History - Overview: Roman Britain, 43 - 410 AD

pageData.title: The Bosporan Kingdom
pageData.titleline: The Bosporan Kingdom - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Bosporan Kingdom. The Bosporan Kingdom was the ancient world's northern frontier - a Greco-Scythian state on the straits of Kerch, between Crimea and the Taman Peninsula, that survived for nearly a thousand years (c. 438 BC - c. AD 527), longer than almost any state of classical antiquity. It grew out of Greek colonies like Panticapaeum that had planted themselves on the Black Sea to tap the riches of the steppe.
pageData.para2: Under the Spartocid dynasty the kingdom took its distinctive double nature: its rulers called themselves archons (elected magistrates) to their Greek citizens and kings to their Scythian subjects - a fusion some historians call the first truly Hellenistic state. Its wealth rested on the export of wheat, fish, and slaves: Bosporan grain fed the cities of Greece, and the kingdom was dubbed 'the Jewel of the Black Sea.' Its rich Greek cities - Panticapaeum above all, but also Phanagoria, Nymphaeum, and Gorgippia - ringed the straits on both shores.
pageData.para3: Its kurgans - the burial mounds of its Greco-Sarmatian elite - have yielded some of the most spectacular goldwork of the ancient world, now the glory of the Hermitage Museum: Greek vases, Scythian gold, and jewelry showing how completely Greek and steppe cultures had merged on this frontier.
pageData.para4: From 63 BC the Bosporan kingdom survived as Rome's longest-lived client kingdom, enjoying a new golden age in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD; King Sauromates II even crushed the Scythians and took all Crimea. It endured the Goths and outlasted the Western Empire before fading in the age of the Huns - a Greek city-world that held the edge of the steppe for a millennium.

pageData.title: The Dacians
pageData.titleline: The Dacians - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Dacians. The Dacians - the Getae of Greek writers - were the people of the Carpathians, the ancient inhabitants of modern Romania, and the most formidable opponents Rome faced on the lower Danube. Close kin of the Thracians, influenced by Scythians and Celts, they lived in fortified hill settlements around their mountain capital of Sarmizegetusa, rich in gold, silver, and iron.
pageData.para2: They had beaten off invaders before: Alexander the Great attacked the Getae on the lower Danube in 335 BC, and in the 1st century BC they drove the Celtic Boii out of their lands. Then King Burebista united the Dacian tribes into a single kingdom - the first Dacian state strong enough to make Rome take notice. The clash came a century later: the emperor Trajan fought two hard Dacian Wars (AD 101-106), commemorated scene by scene on Trajan's Column in Rome, and conquered the kingdom, taking its capital and its gold.
pageData.para3: Dacia became a Roman province - Transylvania and the lands east to the Olt river - settled by colonists from across the empire, though the Romans held only about half the wider Dacian region. The Dacians revolted repeatedly (in 117 and again in 158), and the 'Free Dacians' beyond the frontier, later known as the Carpi, fought Rome for another century and more.
pageData.para4: The Dacians are the remembered ancestors of a modern nation: Romanians trace their name and language to Rome's Dacian province and their roots to the people Rome conquered there. Dacia's mountains still guard the ruins of Sarmizegetusa, the Dacian capital high in the Carpathians, and the wolf-headed dragon standard of Dacian warriors still flies - carved on Trajan's Column - as their emblem.
pageData.source3label: National Geographic: Ancient Transylvanians Rich in Gold, Treasure Shows

pageData.title: The Etruscans
pageData.titleline: The Etruscans - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Etruscans. The Etruscans were ancient Italy's first great civilization - the sophisticated, mysterious people who ruled central Italy before Rome and taught the Romans much of what they knew. From about 900 BC, out of the local Iron Age Villanovan culture, a distinctive Etruscan civilization grew up in Etruria - roughly modern Tuscany, whose very name comes from them - organized not as an empire but as a league of rich, rival city-states: Tarquinia, Veii, Cerveteri, Vulci, and others.
pageData.para2: At their height around 500 BC, the Etruscans dominated Italy from the Po Valley to Campania, and even ruled Rome itself - Rome's last kings, the Tarquins, were Etruscan. Their merchants traded with Greeks and Celts, their sailors commanded the Tyrrhenian Sea (which still bears their Greek name), and their elites filled painted family tombs with imported luxuries. They wrote in an alphabet borrowed from the Greeks - yet their language, unrelated to any other in Europe, is still only partly understood, so we see them mostly through their dazzling tombs and through hostile Roman sources.
pageData.para3: Rome learned from them and then devoured them. From the Etruscans Rome took the arch, the gladiatorial games, religious divination, the symbols of magistrates' power - and, some say, the toga. But beginning in the late 4th century BC, in the long Roman-Etruscan Wars, the cities fell one by one; by 90 BC the Etruscans were Roman citizens, and by the time of Augustus their language was dying.
pageData.para4: The Etruscans vanished into Rome so completely that their own literature is lost. But their influence never died: they stand behind Roman religion, engineering, and statecraft - and so behind the whole Roman Empire. Tuscany's painted tombs remain our window onto the people who made Rome possible.
pageData.source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: 2.1: The Etruscans, an introduction

pageData.title: The Hellenistic Kingdoms
pageData.titleline: The Hellenistic Kingdoms - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Hellenistic Kingdoms. When Alexander the Great died at Babylon in 323 BC, his generals tore his empire apart. Out of forty years of wars between these 'Successors' (the Diadochi) emerged the Hellenistic kingdoms - Greek-ruled states stretching from Greece to India: the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Seleucids in Asia, the Antigonids in Macedon, and later Pergamon, Greco-Bactria, and even an Indo-Greek kingdom on the Indus.
pageData.para2: For three centuries these kingdoms made Greek the world's shared culture. Greeks emigrated by the hundreds of thousands to new cities named for kings - Alexandria, Antioch, Seleucia - and a common Greek dialect, Koine, became the lingua franca from Sicily to India, the language in which the Septuagint and later the New Testament would be written. Local cultures fused with Greek ones: Egyptian gods became Greco-Egyptian Serapis, and in Bactria Greek art met Buddhism.
pageData.para3: The Hellenistic age was also antiquity's greatest age of science and learning. Alexandria's Library and Museum drew the world's scholars: Euclid wrote his Elements and Archimedes his physics there. Its art - the Venus de Milo, the Dying Gaul, the Pergamon Altar - prized drama and emotion over classical calm, and its philosophies - Stoicism, Epicureanism - taught individuals how to live in a world too big for the old city-state.
pageData.para4: The kingdoms fell one by one to Rome: Macedon and Greece by 146 BC, the Seleucid remnant soon after, and finally Cleopatra's Egypt after Actium in 31-30 BC, ending the Hellenistic age. But Greek culture did not fall: the Roman Empire itself ran partly in Greek, and the eastern half of Rome's world remained Greek for another thousand years - the Hellenistic world's longest afterlife.
pageData.source4label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Pergamon and the Hellenistic Kingdoms of the Ancient World: Three Centuries of Greek Art from Alexander the Great to Cleopatra

pageData.title: The Roman Kingdom, Republic, & Empire
pageData.titleline: The Roman Kingdom, Republic, & Empire - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Roman Kingdom, Republic, and Empire. Rome's story runs through three constitutions over twelve centuries: a small kingdom, a conquering republic, and a world empire. Tradition dates the Kingdom from Rome's founding by Romulus in 753 BC: seven kings - the later ones Etruscan - ruled the growing city until 509 BC, when, according to Roman tradition, the tyranny of Tarquin the Proud provoked a revolution that expelled the kings forever. (Modern scholars see a more complicated story behind the legend - but the Romans' hatred of kings was real, and it shaped everything that followed.)
pageData.para2: The Republic (509-27 BC) made Rome master of the Mediterranean. Governed by annually elected consuls, the Senate, and citizen assemblies - and at near-perpetual war - Rome conquered Italy, destroyed its great rival Carthage in three Punic Wars (Hannibal's invasion included), and by 146 BC stood dominant from Spain to Greece. But conquest broke the Republic: wealth and slaves flooded in, generals raised personal armies, and a century of civil strife - reformers against the oligarchy, Marius against Sulla, slave revolts against the legions - ended with Julius Caesar crossing the Rubicon in 49 BC. Victorious but assassinated in 44 BC, Caesar left the stage to his heir Octavian, who defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium and, in 27 BC, took the name Augustus.
pageData.para3: The Empire Augustus founded lasted five hundred years in the West - and, as Byzantium, fifteen hundred in the East. Its first two centuries, the Pax Romana, brought the Mediterranean world unprecedented peace and prosperity: across Europe, North Africa, and Western Asia, tens of millions of people shared Roman roads, Roman law, and Roman cities. Under Trajan the empire reached its greatest extent, some 5 million square kilometers.
pageData.para4: Crisis came in the 3rd century - civil wars, plagues, invasions - before Diocletian reorganized and Constantine turned the empire Christian and moved its capital to Constantinople. The Western Empire fell to Germanic kings in 476; the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire endured until 1453. Rome's legacy is the West's foundation: its law, its languages, its roads, its calendar - and the very idea of a world ruled from one city.

pageData.title: The Sarmatians
pageData.titleline: The Sarmatians - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Sarmatians. The Sarmatians - first mentioned, as 'Sairima', in the Zoroastrian Avesta - were the successors of the Scythians - the Iranian nomad confederation that ruled the Pontic steppe from around the 5th century BC to the 4th century AD, six hundred years of steppe empire. Like the Scythians, they were horse archers and cattle herders; their confederation brought together the great tribes of the steppe: the Aorsi, the Roxolani, the Iazyges, and above all the Alans.
pageData.para2: Moving west from the steppes between the Urals and the Don, the Sarmatians overwhelmed the Scythians by about 200 BC, and at their greatest extent, around 100 BC, their tribes ranged from the Danube to the Volga. Moving ever westward, they absorbed or drove out the peoples before them: the Iazyges settled on the Tisza plain in modern Hungary, the Roxolani on the lower Danube, and the Alans built a confederation stretching from the Caucasus toward the Urals.
pageData.para3: From the 1st century AD, Sarmatian tribes pressed against Rome's Danube frontier - the Iazyges and Roxolani attacked Moesia and Thrace, and Roman governors fought to hold the river line. But the steppe world was ending: the Goths broke Sarmatian power in the 3rd century, and the Hunnic invasions of the 4th finished it. Many Sarmatians then joined the Goths and other Germanic peoples and rode west into the falling Roman Empire.
pageData.para4: The Sarmatians vanished as a people - absorbed by Goths, Huns, Slavs, and the peoples of the Caucasus - but one branch survived: the Alans held out in the North Caucasus into the Middle Ages and gave rise to the modern Ossetians, who still speak a descendant of the Sarmatians' Iranian tongue.

pageData.title: The Scythians
pageData.titleline: The Scythians - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Scythians. The Scythians were the first great nation of the steppe - the Iranian-speaking horse nomads who dominated the grasslands north of the Black Sea from the 9th to the 3rd century BC and terrified the civilized world. Migrating from Central Asia to the Pontic Steppe (modern Ukraine and southern Russia), they displaced the Cimmerians and built a warrior society in which wealth, war, and status all came from the horse.
pageData.para2: The Scythians were the terror of empires. In the 7th century BC they swept over the Caucasus and raided deep into the Near East; in 513 BC the Persian king Darius I invaded Scythia with a huge army - and failed completely, as the Scythians simply vanished into the steppe, drawing the Persians after them until hunger forced retreat. It was a lesson no empire ever forgot: you cannot conquer people who have no cities to take.
pageData.para3: Greek colonists on the Black Sea - above all Herodotus, our main source - traded with them, wrote about them, and marveled at them: the royal burials in great mounds (kurgans) filled with gold, the sacrificed horses, the warrior women who may lie behind the Amazon legends. Scythian gold - animal-style art of stags, griffins, and combat - remains among the most spectacular art of the ancient world.
pageData.para4: Their end came from their own kin: in the 3rd century BC the related Sarmatians drove the Scythians from the steppe, and the remnants dwindled into small kingdoms in Crimea and on the lower Danube. But their way of war - mounted archery on the open grassland - outlived them for two thousand years: every steppe horde that followed, down to the Mongols, rode in the Scythians' path.

pageData.title: The Thracians
pageData.titleline: The Thracians - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Thracians. The Thracians were the ancient people of the southeastern Balkans - the lands of modern Bulgaria, northern Greece, and European Turkey - famed across the ancient world as fierce warriors, superb horsemen, and musicians, yet never united enough to found a lasting empire. Greek writers called them numerous and warlike, and Thracian horsemen were famous from Homer onward - the Iliad gives them King Rhesus and his snow-white horses. The cult of Orpheus, the legendary musician, flourished in their lands.
pageData.para2: Thracian culture was old - flourishing from the Bronze Age - but politically the tribes stayed divided until the early 5th century BC, when King Teres I founded the Odrysian kingdom in the vacuum left by Persia's failed invasion of Greece. Under Teres and his son Sitalces it became one of the most powerful states of its day, allied with Athens in the Peloponnesian War; but after 400 BC it weakened, and around 340 BC Philip of Macedon absorbed it.
pageData.para3: Thracian nobles went to their graves with their horses and chariots, to serve them in the afterlife - a custom their tombs still attest. And their treasures tell the story their lack of writing cannot: only four Thracian inscriptions survive, but the goldwork found in Bulgarian soil shows a rich, sophisticated aristocratic culture trading with Greece and Persia alike.
pageData.para4: Rome swallowed Thrace slowly: from the mid-2nd century BC the region slid under Roman power, and in AD 45-46 the last client kingdom became the province of Thracia. The Thracians Romanized and disappeared as a distinct people - but they had already given the ancient world two of its most famous rebels and heroes, and the Bulgarians, Greeks, and Turks of today walk on their tombs.

pageData.title: The Minoan Civilization
pageData.titleline: The Minoan Civilization - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Minoan civilization (c. 3100-1100 BCE) was Europe's first major literate-age civilization, centered on the island of Crete in the southern Aegean. Named by the archaeologist Arthur Evans after the legendary King Minos, it emerged from farming communities settled on Crete in the Neolithic period and grew into a network of palace-centered towns. Around 1900 BCE the first great palaces appeared at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros, marking what scholars call the First Palace Period. The Minoans developed writing systems known as Cretan hieroglyphic and Linear A, which remain largely undeciphered, so their history is reconstructed mostly from archaeology.
pageData.para2: Palace society reached its height between about 1700 and 1450 BCE. The rebuilt palaces were large multi-storey complexes with storage magazines, workshops, ceremonial courts and advanced drainage, decorated with vivid frescoes of processions, plants, animals and bull-leaping. The palaces acted as economic hubs: scribes recorded harvests, herds and craft production, and storerooms held grain, oil and wine. Minoan traders ranged across the eastern Mediterranean, exchanging pottery, textiles and metals with Egypt, Syria, Cyprus and the Greek mainland, and Cretan goods and styles spread widely through the Aegean islands.
pageData.para3: Minoan religion centered on a principal goddess or goddesses associated with nature, animals and household cult, worshipped at peak sanctuaries, sacred caves and palace shrines. The double axe and the bull were central symbols, and bull-leaping appears both in art and, apparently, in ritual sport held in the palace courts. Society seems to have been comparatively peaceful: Minoan towns lacked heavy fortifications, and art emphasizes ceremony, sport and seafaring rather than warfare. Workshops produced fine stone vases, seal stones, gold jewelry and elegant pottery such as Kamares ware, admired and imitated abroad.
pageData.para4: Around 1450 BCE most Minoan palaces and towns were destroyed, a catastrophe still debated by scholars. The huge eruption of Thera (Santorini), dated to the later 16th century BCE, damaged Crete's northern coast and shipping, and may have weakened the palaces, but it did not end the civilization by itself. After 1450 BCE, Greek-speaking Mycenaeans took over Knossos and much of the island, keeping palace records in Linear B, an early form of Greek. Knossos finally collapsed around 1200-1100 BCE amid the wider Bronze Age crisis, but Minoan craftsmanship, religion and seafaring strongly shaped later Greek culture.

pageData.title: The Greek Dark Ages and Archaic Colonization
pageData.titleline: The Greek Dark Ages and Archaic Colonization - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Greek Dark Ages (c. 1100-750 BCE) followed the collapse of the Mycenaean palace kingdoms around 1200 BCE, when destructions, migrations and the breakdown of trade emptied the great citadels of Mycenae, Tiryns and Pylos. Writing in Linear B disappeared, monumental building stopped, and the population of Greece fell sharply. Communities became smaller, poorer and more mobile, and long-distance exchange with Egypt and the Near East contracted. Our picture of these centuries comes almost entirely from archaeology, since the Greeks of this era left no written records of their own.
pageData.para2: Life slowly recovered. Iron gradually replaced bronze for tools and weapons, and new styles of painted pottery, first Protogeometric and then Geometric, show growing skill and contact between regions. Traditionally dated movements of Greek-speaking peoples, including the Dorians into the Peloponnese and Aeolians and Ionians across the Aegean to the coast of Asia Minor, gave the Greek world its lasting regional dialect map. By the 9th century BCE some communities, above all Athens and the Euboean towns, were again wealthy enough to trade with Cyprus and the Levant, as finds from the cemetery at Lefkandi show.
pageData.para3: From about 750 BCE Greeks began founding colonies across the Mediterranean and Black Seas, a movement driven by land hunger, trade and political tension at home. Euboeans settled Pithekoussai and Cumae in Italy, Corinthians founded Syracuse and Corcyra, Megarians planted towns on the Bosporus, and Miletus and Phocaea sent settlers to the Black Sea and the far west. Colonies were independent poleis, not possessions, but they kept cult and kinship ties with their mother cities. Through them, Greek goods, alphabetic writing, adapted from the Phoenician script, and Greek religious practice spread far beyond the Aegean.
pageData.para4: The recovery of the 8th century BCE created the world of the classical polis. Population grew, villages merged into city-states, and shared sanctuaries such as Olympia and Delphi linked the scattered Greek communities through festivals, games and oracles. The same era produced the Homeric epics, which gave Greeks a common heroic past, and the hoplite style of fighting that underpinned citizen armies. Colonization and trade enriched new classes who challenged old aristocracies, setting up the political struggles, and the lawgivers and tyrants, of the following Archaic age.
pageData.source1label: World History Encyclopedia: Greek Dark Age

pageData.title: The Athenian Empire and the Peloponnesian War
pageData.titleline: The Athenian Empire and the Peloponnesian War - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Athenian Empire (478-404 BCE) grew out of the Delian League, a voluntary alliance of Greek city-states founded in 478 BCE on the island of Delos to continue the war against Persia after the victories of 480-479 BCE. Athens supplied most of the fleet and its generals, while allies contributed ships or, increasingly, annual payments of silver called phoros. Early campaigns under Cimon drove Persian forces from the Aegean and won a major victory at the Eurymedon River around 466 BCE, but Athens soon used league power against league members who tried to leave, turning allies into subjects.
pageData.para2: The transformation into empire became unmistakable in 454 BCE, when the league treasury was moved from Delos to Athens. Athenian democracy under Pericles spent the tribute on the city's fleet, on pay for jurors and rowers, and on the great building program of the Acropolis, including the Parthenon. Athens installed garrisons and democratic governments, seized land for Athenian settlers called cleruchs, and required major legal cases of allies to be heard in Athenian courts. Control of the sea brought control of the grain routes from the Black Sea, on which Athens' large population depended.
pageData.para3: Rivalry with Sparta and its Peloponnesian League broke into open conflict in 431 BCE, beginning the Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE). Pericles' strategy avoided land battles with Sparta's superior hoplites and relied on the Long Walls and the fleet, but a plague in 430 BCE killed a large share of Athens' crowded population, including Pericles himself. After ten years of fighting, the Peace of Nicias (421 BCE) gave only a pause. In 415 BCE Athens launched a huge expedition against Syracuse in Sicily, which ended in 413 BCE with the destruction of the entire armada, the war's decisive disaster.
pageData.para4: Persian money then rebuilt Sparta's fleet, while Athens' empire began to revolt. Under the general Lysander, Sparta won at Aegospotami in 405 BCE, destroying the last Athenian fleet, and starved Athens into surrender in 404 BCE. The empire was dissolved, the Long Walls demolished, and a Spartan-backed oligarchy, the Thirty Tyrants, briefly ruled the city. Democracy was restored within a year, and Athens later rebuilt much of its naval power through the Second Athenian League of 377 BCE, but it never again dominated Greece. The war weakened all the city-states and opened the way first to Spartan, then Theban, and finally Macedonian hegemony.

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Macedon and Alexander's Successors
pageData.titleline: The Kingdom of Macedon and Alexander's Successors - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Macedon (c. 700-168 BCE) occupied the plains and mountains north of classical Greece, ruled by the Argead dynasty, which claimed descent from Argos. Long a frontier kingdom of herders and warriors, Macedon was drawn into Greek affairs by kings such as Archelaus, who moved the court to Pella and patronized Greek artists. Real power came with Philip II (reigned 359-336 BCE), who created a professional army built around the sarissa phalanx and companion cavalry, seized gold-rich Mount Pangaeum, and used war, diplomacy and marriage to dominate Thessaly, Thrace and the Greek cities.
pageData.para2: After defeating Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, Philip organized the League of Corinth, a Greek alliance under Macedonian leadership, and prepared an invasion of the Persian Empire. He was assassinated in 336 BCE, and his twenty-year-old son Alexander III inherited the project. In thirteen years Alexander conquered Asia Minor, Egypt, Syria, Mesopotamia and Persia itself, reaching the Indus before his army refused to go further. When he died at Babylon in 323 BCE without an adult heir, he left the largest empire the Mediterranean world had seen, and no plan for holding it together.
pageData.para3: Alexander's generals, the Diadochi or 'Successors', fought more than forty years of wars over his inheritance. Infantry and fleet, treasury and even the king's corpse became weapons in their struggles, which ended the Argead line entirely. By the settlement reached after the battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE, three great Hellenistic kingdoms had crystallized: the Antigonids in Macedon and Greece, the Ptolemies in Egypt, and the Seleucids in Asia. In these courts Greek became the language of government and culture from the Nile to Central Asia, and cities such as Alexandria, Antioch and Pergamon became centers of learning, trade and royal patronage.
pageData.para4: Macedon itself recovered under Antigonus II Gonatas, who secured the throne in 276 BCE and gave the kingdom a stable dynasty. Antigonid kings ruled through alliances and garrisons in Greece while fending off Celtic invasions and Illyrian raiders. Conflict with expanding Rome proved fatal: Philip V was defeated at Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE, and his son Perseus lost the kingdom at Pydna in 168 BCE. Rome abolished the monarchy and divided Macedon into four republics, and after the revolt of Andriscus it became a Roman province in 146 BCE. Macedon's legacy endured in the Hellenistic kingdoms, whose Greek-speaking courts shaped the eastern Mediterranean for centuries.
pageData.source3label: World History Encyclopedia: Wars of the Diadochi

pageData.title: Rome and the Greek World
pageData.titleline: Rome and the Greek World - The History Web
pageData.para1: Rome's entanglement with the Greek world (280-31 BCE) began in Italy itself, where Greek colonies of Magna Graecia had flourished for centuries. When Rome pressured the city of Tarentum, its people called in King Pyrrhus of Epirus, who defeated Roman armies at Heraclea (280 BCE) and Asculum (279 BCE) at such cost that his victories became proverbial. Pyrrhus withdrew in 275 BCE, and by 272 BCE Tarentum fell, giving Rome control of the Greek south of Italy. The Punic Wars then made Rome master of Sicily, its first province, with the Greek city of Syracuse captured in 212 BCE despite the defenses devised by Archimedes.
pageData.para2: Rome next intervened across the Adriatic, where the Antigonid kings of Macedon and the leagues of Greece struggled for advantage. Philip V of Macedon had allied with Hannibal, and Rome answered with the Second Macedonian War: at Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE the Roman legion under Titus Quinctius Flamininus broke the Macedonian phalanx. Flamininus theatrically declared the 'freedom of the Greeks' at the Isthmian Games of 196 BCE, and Rome defeated the Seleucid king Antiochus III at Magnesia in 189 BCE, forcing him from Asia Minor. Yet Rome's protector role steadily hardened into domination as Greek states appealed to it in their quarrels.
pageData.para3: In 171 BCE war resumed against Philip's son Perseus, whose defeat at Pydna in 168 BCE ended the Macedonian monarchy. Rome deported a thousand leading Achaeans, including the historian Polybius, and grew impatient with Greek politics. When the Achaean League fought Sparta and defied Roman orders, a Roman army under Lucius Mummius crushed it and destroyed Corinth in 146 BCE, the same year Carthage fell; Greece was placed under the oversight of the governor of Macedonia. The rich kingdom of Pergamon was willed to Rome in 133 BCE and became the province of Asia, and by the 1st century BCE the whole Aegean paid Roman taxes.
pageData.para4: Greece suffered again as a theater of Rome's civil wars: Sulla sacked Athens in 86 BCE after it sided with Mithridates VI of Pontus, and the battles of Pharsalus (48 BCE), Philippi (42 BCE) and finally Actium (31 BCE), off the Greek coast, decided the fate of the Republic. Yet conquest reversed culturally. Greek language, literature, philosophy, art and education captivated the Roman elite, who studied in Athens and staffed their households with Greek teachers and doctors. The poet Horace summed it up: captive Greece captured her savage conqueror. Under the Empire, Greece became the peaceful province of Achaea, its cities honored as the wellsprings of classical culture.
pageData.source4label: World History Encyclopedia: Titus Quinctius Flamininus

pageData.title: The Illyrians
pageData.titleline: The Illyrians - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Illyrians (c. 1000 BCE-168 BCE) were a group of related Indo-European peoples who occupied the western Balkans, from the Danube basin down the Adriatic coast to Epirus. Ancient writers used 'Illyrian' loosely for many tribes, including the Ardiaei, Dardani, Taulantii, Liburni, Dalmatae and Pannonii, who shared languages and customs but never formed a single nation. They lived in hilltop settlements, raised livestock, mined silver and iron, and were famed as warriors and sailors. Greek colonists founded trading towns such as Epidamnus and Apollonia on their coasts in the 7th-6th centuries BCE, through which Greek goods, coins and ideas entered the interior.
pageData.para2: From the 5th century BCE some tribes formed short-lived kingdoms. Bardylis of the Dardani defeated the Macedonians and Molossians around 393 BCE and seized parts of upper Macedonia before Philip II crushed the Illyrians in 358 BCE, securing his kingdom's western frontier. Further south, King Agron of the Ardiaei built the strongest Illyrian state in the 3rd century BCE, with a fleet of light, fast galleys called lembi that raided and traded across the Adriatic. His widow Queen Teuta continued the attacks on Italian shipping, which brought her into direct collision with Rome.
pageData.para3: Rome's First Illyrian War (229-228 BCE) broke Teuta's power, and the Second (219 BCE) drove out her successor Demetrius of Pharos, giving Rome a protectorate over the Illyrian coast. The kingdom revived under Genthius, who allied with Macedon during the Third Macedonian War; in 168 BCE a Roman praetor captured him at Scodra, and Rome split the Illyrian kingdom into three client republics. Repeated rebellions followed until, after hard campaigns in 35-33 BCE and the Great Illyrian Revolt of 6-9 CE, the whole region became the Roman provinces of Dalmatia and Pannonia.
pageData.para4: Under Rome the Illyrians were heavily Romanized: soldiers recruited in the Balkans rose to command armies, and several 3rd-century emperors, including Claudius II, Aurelian, Probus and Diocletian, who retired to a vast palace at Split, were of Illyrian origin. Latin displaced native speech along the coast and in the towns, while older languages survived longer in the mountains. Linguists long linked the Illyrians to the later Albanians, though the exact relationship remains debated. Their hillforts, tumulus graves, silver coinage and distinctive helmets still mark the archaeology of the western Balkans.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Illyria - Exploring Ancient Albania

pageData.title: The Lusitanian Wars
pageData.titleline: The Lusitanian Wars - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Lusitanian Wars (155-139 BCE) were a series of hard-fought campaigns between the Roman Republic and the Lusitani, a collection of tribes living west of the Tagus in what is now Portugal. Rome had been in Iberia since the Second Punic War, and its governors squeezed the mountain peoples with raids, tribute demands and land seizures. The Lusitani, cattle-herders and fighters organized in war bands, answered with guerrilla tactics: ambushes in the passes, sudden descents on Roman columns, and rapid dispersal into rough country where heavy legions could not follow.
pageData.para2: Open war began in 155 BCE when the Lusitani defeated two Roman armies and crossed into Baetica. Their greatest leader emerged in 147 BCE: Viriathus, a shepherd and hunter who had survived the treacherous massacres ordered by the praetor Galba in 150 BCE. A gifted guerrilla commander, Viriathus won victory after victory over eight years, defeating five Roman commanders, seizing towns, and extending the war across central Iberia by inspiring the Celtiberians to rise as well. At Tribola he trapped a consular army, and Rome was humiliated into recognizing him in 141 BCE as 'a friend and ally of the Roman people'.
pageData.para3: That peace was the work of the consul Fabius Maximus Servilianus, whom Viriathus had trapped and then released after negotiating terms. The Roman Senate, however, refused to accept an equal treaty with a guerrilla leader. Fabius' brother and successor, Quintus Servilius Caepio, resumed the war, pressed the Lusitani hard, and finally bribed three of Viriathus' own companions, Audax, Ditalcus and Minurus, to murder their leader in his sleep in 139 BCE. The story goes that when the killers claimed their reward, they were told that Rome did not pay traitors.
pageData.para4: Leaderless, the Lusitani surrendered, and Caepio deported survivors to settled communities where they could be watched. The Celtiberian resistance lasted until the fall of Numantia in 133 BCE, and the far northwest was not subdued until Augustus' Cantabrian Wars ending in 19 BCE. Rome then organized the territory as the province of Lusitania, with its capital at Emerita Augusta (Merida). Viriathus became Iberia's enduring symbol of resistance: Roman historians themselves praised his justice, austerity and leadership, and later Portuguese and Spanish tradition honored him as a national hero before either nation existed.

pageData.title: The Huns
pageData.titleline: The Huns - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Huns (c. 370-469 CE) were a nomadic people of the Eurasian steppe who burst into European history around 370 CE, when they crossed the Volga, crushed the Alans, and defeated the Gothic kingdom of Ermanaric near the Dniester. Mounted archers raised in the saddle, they moved with herds and wagons and fought with the powerful composite bow, striking at a speed settled peoples could not match. Their origin is debated: some scholars link them to the Xiongnu of the Chinese sources, others see a new steppe confederation, and their language remains unknown. Their advance pushed Goths, Vandals and other peoples across Rome's frontiers, setting the age of migrations in motion.
pageData.para2: For two generations the Huns operated as raiders and as mercenaries for hire by both Romans and their enemies, while subjugating the peoples between the Black Sea and Central Europe. Under King Rua they began extracting regular tribute from the Eastern Roman Empire. In 434 CE power passed jointly to his nephews Bleda and Attila, who soon forced Constantinople to triple its payments. After Bleda's death around 445, Attila ruled alone over an empire stretching from the Caspian to the Rhine, demanding gold, fugitives and market access with the threat of war.
pageData.para3: Attila's wars reached their peak in the 440s and early 450s. His armies ravaged the Balkans in 441-443 and 447, destroying cities and advancing to Constantinople's walls, though they never took the city's defenses by storm. In 451 he invaded Gaul, besieging Orleans, before a coalition of Romans under Aetius and Visigoths under Theodoric I met him on the Catalaunian Fields; after enormous slaughter on both sides the Huns withdrew, the only major check Attila suffered. The next year he invaded Italy, sacked Aquileia and Milan, and turned back short of Rome after disease, hunger and an embassy led by Pope Leo I.
pageData.para4: Attila died suddenly in 453 CE, on the night of his wedding to a new bride, reportedly from a hemorrhage. His many sons divided the empire and fell to quarreling, and in 454 their subject peoples, led by the Gepid king Ardaric, destroyed Hunnic power at the battle of the Nedao. The remnants were absorbed or pushed back to the Pontic steppe within a generation. The Huns left few monuments and no writings, but their impact was enormous: they shattered the balance of power on Rome's frontiers, accelerated the collapse of the Western Empire, and entered legend from the Nibelungenlied to Hungarian tradition as the archetype of the steppe conqueror.
pageData.source3label: World History Encyclopedia: Attila the Hun

pageData.title: The Late Roman Empire and the Barbarian Invasions
pageData.titleline: The Late Roman Empire and the Barbarian Invasions - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Late Roman Empire began with Diocletian (reigned 284-305 CE), who pulled the state out of the crisis of the third century by reorganizing the army, provinces and taxation, and by sharing power in the tetrarchy, a system of two senior and two junior emperors. Constantine I (306-337) reunited the empire, granted Christians legal toleration in 313, and founded Constantinople in 330 as a new capital on the Bosporus. The late empire was still populous and wealthy, but it faced persistent pressure on the Rhine, Danube and Persian frontiers, and civil wars repeatedly diverted the field armies that guarded them.
pageData.para2: In 376 CE the Goths, fleeing the Huns, were admitted across the Danube by the eastern emperor Valens; mistreated by Roman officials, they revolted and destroyed Valens and his army at Adrianople in 378, a shock from which Roman prestige never fully recovered. From 395 the empire was permanently administered in eastern and western halves. Germanic commanders rose to dominate western politics, and on the last night of 406 Vandals, Suebi and Alans crossed the frozen Rhine and devastated Gaul. In 410 the Visigoths under Alaric sacked Rome itself, and the western court at Ravenna survived largely by bargaining with the warlords who now commanded its armies.
pageData.para3: During the fifth century the western provinces were carved into successor kingdoms. The Visigoths settled in Aquitaine and then conquered most of Spain; the Vandals under Genseric crossed to Africa in 429, took Carthage in 439 and built a fleet with which they sacked Rome in 455; the Burgundians and Franks divided Gaul; Angles, Saxons and Jutes occupied a Britain abandoned by the legions. Attila's Huns extracted tribute from both halves of the empire before his death in 453. Emperors in the west became puppets of Germanic generals such as Ricimer, while the east, richer and better defended, held its own.
pageData.para4: In 476 CE the general Odoacer deposed the young western emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, ruling Italy in the eastern emperor's name. The date conventionally marks the end of the Western Roman Empire, though contemporaries saw Odoacer's Italy and the new kingdoms as still belonging to a Roman world. The Eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire survived another thousand years, reconquering Italy, Africa and parts of Spain under Justinian in the 6th century. The barbarian successor kingdoms, meanwhile, preserved much Roman law, administration and Christian culture, and became the foundations of medieval Europe.

pageData.title: The Early Slavs
pageData.titleline: The Early Slavs - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Early Slavs (c. 500-1000 CE) emerge into written history in the 6th century, when Byzantine authors such as Procopius and Jordanes describe peoples called Sclaveni and Antes raiding across the Danube. Their earlier homeland is placed by most scholars between the Vistula and the Dnieper, in the forest and marsh country of present-day Poland, Ukraine and Belarus. They lived in small villages, farmed with simple plows, kept livestock, and organized themselves in kin groups and tribal assemblies without kings. Archaeologists associate them with modest handmade pottery and sunken-floor huts, material so plain that early Slavic settlements are hard to trace.
pageData.para2: From the later 6th century Slavic groups expanded in every direction, often in the shadow of the Avar khaganate, whose horsemen dominated the Danube plain. They flooded into the Balkans, besieging Thessalonica and settling permanently in Greece; they spread west to the Elbe and the Baltic, and east into the Russian forests, where they mixed with Baltic and Finnic peoples. By the 7th century Slavs formed the majority population over most of eastern and central Europe. New polities soon appeared: the Samo realm (c. 623-658), the first known Slavic 'kingdom', resisted both Avars and Franks, and Carantania and Great Moravia followed.
pageData.para3: Slavic religion was polytheistic, centered on gods of sky, storm and fertility such as Perun and Veles, with sacred groves, springs and carved idols rather than temples. Conversion came gradually. In 863 the brothers Cyril and Methodius from Thessalonica began preaching to Great Moravia in the Slavic vernacular, devising the Glagolitic alphabet, ancestor of Cyrillic, to translate scripture and law. Their mission, welcomed in Moravia but opposed by Frankish clergy, planted Slavic literacy that later flourished in Bulgaria, Serbia and Rus'. Political Christianization followed: the Bohemian and Polish dukes accepted Latin Christianity in the 10th century, Bulgaria in 864, and the Rus' of Kiev under Vladimir in 988.
pageData.para4: The early Slavs left a deep mark on Europe's map and languages. Their descendants form the largest European language family group, from Polish, Czech and Croatian to Bulgarian, Ukrainian and Russian. Slavic settlement redrew the ethnic geography of the Balkans and the east European plain, and the first Slavic states, Moravia, Bohemia, Poland, Bulgaria and Kievan Rus', became the enduring political nations of eastern Europe. Villages, open-field farming and a strong oral tradition of epic and song characterized their culture, while their adoption of Christianity in both its Latin and Byzantine forms tied different Slavic peoples to Europe's two Christian worlds.

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Epirus
pageData.titleline: The Kingdom of Epirus - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Epirus occupied the mountainous northwest of Greece, facing Italy across the narrowest stretch of the Adriatic. Its tribes, including the Molossians, Thesprotians and Chaonians, spoke Greek and worshipped at Dodona, home of the famous oracle of Zeus, whose priests interpreted the rustling of a sacred oak. Long organized in loose tribal leagues, Epirus was unified as a kingdom around 430-370 BCE under the Molossian dynasty, which traced its descent from Achilles. King Alexander I (342-331 BCE) expanded his power and died campaigning in Italy, and his sister Olympias married Philip II of Macedon and became the mother of Alexander the Great.
pageData.para2: Epirus' most famous ruler was Pyrrhus (reigned 307-302 and 297-272 BCE), a brilliant, restless general trained in the wars of Alexander's successors. Twice driven from his throne, he fought in Egypt and Greece, and in 280 BCE answered the call of Tarentum to lead the Greek cities of Italy against Rome. At Heraclea (280) and Asculum (279) he beat the legions with war elephants and his elite phalanx, but his heavy losses, 'another such victory and we are undone', gave the world the phrase 'Pyrrhic victory'. He then campaigned in Sicily against Carthage (278-276) with initial success before Greek allies turned against him, and returned to Italy only to be checked by Rome at Beneventum in 275 BCE.
pageData.para3: Back home Pyrrhus seized much of Macedonia and died in 272 BCE in a street fight in Argos, struck down, the story says, by a roof tile thrown by an old woman. His wars exhausted Epirus, and the monarchy declined through the 3rd century. Around 232 BCE the Epirotes abolished the kingship and reorganized as a federal republic, the Epirote League, governed by elected officials. Caught between Rome and Macedon, the league made the fatal choice of siding with Perseus of Macedon.
pageData.para4: When Rome destroyed Macedon at Pydna in 168 BCE, the Senate punished Epirus savagely: Aemilius Paullus' troops systematically sacked seventy towns and carried off, by the ancient account, 150,000 people into slavery. The region never recovered its old importance. Under the Empire, Epirus was a quiet province, though Octavian founded the new city of Nicopolis near Actium to celebrate his victory of 31 BCE. The Epirote example still stood as a warning of what happened to Greek states that chose the wrong side, and Pyrrhus remained the model of the general whose victories cost more than defeats.

pageData.title: Syracuse and Magna Graecia
pageData.titleline: Syracuse and Magna Graecia - The History Web
pageData.para1: Magna Graecia, 'Greater Greece', was the name Romans gave to the Greek colonial world of southern Italy, where settlers from the 8th century BCE onward founded cities such as Sybaris, Croton, Tarentum, Rhegium and Locri, while Chalcidians and Corinthians colonized eastern Sicily. Fertile land and busy trade made cities like Sybaris bywords for wealth and luxury. The region produced some of the earliest Greek lawgivers and philosophers: Pythagoras taught at Croton, Parmenides at Elea, and the Pythagorean communities briefly dominated several cities. The colonies also warred constantly with each other and with their Italic neighbors, the Etruscans, and Carthage.
pageData.para2: Syracuse, founded by Corinthians about 734 BCE on the island of Ortygia, became the greatest Greek city of the west. Under the tyrant Gelon it defeated a huge Carthaginian expedition at Himera in 480 BCE, the same year as Salamis by Greek tradition, and under Hieron I its navy smashed the Etruscans at Cumae (474 BCE). Syracuse's power, wealth and ambitions made it the focus of Athenian imperial dreams: the great Athenian expedition of 415-413 BCE ended in catastrophe in its harbor and quarries, destroying Athens' fleet and army. The city then fell under Dionysius I (405-367 BCE), who built the strongest military monarchy in the Greek world, fought Carthage to a standstill, and walled the heights of Epipolae.
pageData.para3: After Dionysius' death Syracuse swung between tyranny, civil war and brief liberations: the Corinthian Timoleon restored its freedom and crushed Carthage at the Crimisus in 341 BCE, but Agathocles seized power in 317 BCE, took the title of king and carried the war into Africa. His death in 289 BCE brought renewed chaos, Pyrrhus' intervention, and finally the rule of Hieron II (269-215 BCE), under whom the city enjoyed a long, prosperous peace. Syracuse was then a center of science and letters, home to the mathematician Archimedes and the poet Theocritus.
pageData.para4: During the Second Punic War, Hieronymus, Hieron's young grandson, switched Syracuse to the Carthaginian side, and Rome sent Marcus Claudius Marcellus to reduce the city. The siege of 214-212 BCE became legendary for Archimedes' war machines, cranes that lifted ships and mirrors said to have set them ablaze, but hunger and treachery finally opened the gates. Archimedes was killed in the sack, against Marcellus' orders. Syracuse became the capital of the Roman province of Sicily, and Magna Graecia's cities gradually Latinized, though Greek speech survived in southern Italy's remoter corners into the Middle Ages.
